analysis.one_liner: Toughened federal pipeline safety rules with more inspectors, higher fines, mandatory pressure testing, and automatic shutoff valves.
analysis.headline: The bill would have added 100 federal pipeline safety inspectors and raised fines to $250,000 per violation, but it was referred to committee the day it was introduced and never received a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have strengthened federal oversight of the nation's gas and hazardous liquid pipelines. It would have added at least 100 safety inspectors, raised fines to $250,000 for violations tied to deaths, injuries, or major environmental damage, and required pipeline operators to verify the safe maximum pressure of older lines through testing — or replace them. It also would have required automatic or remote-controlled shutoff valves where feasible, regular robotic ("smart pig") inspections in densely populated areas, and brought currently exempt rural gathering lines under federal rules.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live and work near natural gas and hazardous liquid pipelines, especially in densely populated areas, gain stronger inspections, faster leak detection, mandatory shutoff valves, and an enforcement agency with 100 more staff. Communities that would bear the cost of a pipeline explosion or spill, and the environment, are the intended beneficiaries.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Residents near gas and hazardous liquid pipelines

how_it_helps.text: Adds at least 100 full-time staff to the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration, phased in over four years, focused on inspections, data collection, and enforcement support.

Raises civil penalties to up to $250,000 per violation — $2.5 million for a related series — when a violation contributes to a death, a hospitalization, more than $250,000 in environmental damage, or a threatening release in a high-consequence area.
Requires regulations for remotely or automatically controlled valves that can shut off gas flow in an accident, wherever technically and economically feasible.

Requires operators of older natural gas transmission lines to document and verify their maximum allowable operating pressure; where records don't exist, operators must pressure-test or replace the segment and, in the meantime, run at no more than 80% of the highest pressure previously used.

Requires inspection of pipelines in densely populated or environmentally sensitive areas with an internal robotic inspection device at least every five years, with an alternative method where devices can't be used.
Ends the federal safety exemption for rural gas and hazardous liquid gathering lines and extends the definition of hazardous liquids to non-petroleum fuels and biofuels.
Directs the Secretary of Transportation to set standards for natural gas leak detection equipment and methods so substantial leaks in high-consequence areas are found as fast as technology allows.

analysis.who_pays: Pipeline operators — the companies that own and run gas, oil, and hazardous liquid pipelines — would pay through higher fines, mandatory pressure testing and possible pipe replacement, valve installations, five-year inspections, and new fees for design reviews and waiver applications. Some of those costs would likely be passed through to energy customers through rates.
analysis.who_pays_short: Pipeline operators, partly via energy rates

drawbacks.text: The testing and replacement requirements are the bill's costliest mandate: operators of older transmission lines without verifiable records would have up to five years to pressure-test or replace segments, and those compliance costs would likely show up in energy rates.

The bill does not eliminate waivers: operators could still apply to be excused from safety standards for renewable five-year periods, with public notice and comment — a concession that keeps a door open to exemptions.
The shutoff-valve mandate only applies "wherever technically and economically feasible," giving regulators and operators room to limit where valves are actually installed.
New cost-recovery fees for design reviews and waiver processing would be charged to companies proposing pipeline projects, adding to the cost of building new pipeline capacity.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The safety gains target real and serious risks: pipeline failures in populated areas can kill people, and the bill's answer — more inspectors, verified operating pressures, regular internal inspections, and automatic shutoff valves — addresses the known causes. The main costs fall on pipeline operators, though some would reach consumers through rates, and the five-year testing window plus the preserved waiver process soften the mandate. On balance the benefits to public safety outweigh the compliance costs, which is the usual trade-off in safety regulation.

outcome.mechanism: Introduced in late January 2011 and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee the same day, the bill never got a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and it died when the 112th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Dianne Feinstein introduced the bill in the Senate on January 31, 2011, with Senator Barbara Boxer, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation that same day.
The action history shows no further activity: no hearing, no committee markup, no floor vote was ever recorded.
The bill remained pending in committee until the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013, at which point it expired.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Pipeline operators are better off because the bill died: they never faced the higher $250,000-per-violation penalties, mandatory pressure testing or replacement of older lines, required shutoff valves and five-year inspections, or new fees. The promised 100 additional federal safety inspectors and stronger enforcement were never put in place.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Pipeline operators, who avoided new mandates

for.name: Sen. Dianne Feinstein
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill to add 100 pipeline safety inspectors, raise penalties to $250,000 per violation, mandate pressure testing of older lines, and require automatic shutoff valves.

for.name: Sen. Barbara Boxer
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's one cosponsor, named in the introduction.

for.name: Sen. Harry Reid
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on the Senate floor on Feinstein's behalf.

against.name: John D. Rockefeller IV
against.role: Chair, Senate Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee, the bill's committee of referral, took no recorded action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the full two years of the 112th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote ever occurred, so no partisan split is on record; the bill's only two sponsors were both Democrats and no Republican signed on.

industries.note: The bill's core burden falls on companies running gas, oil, and hazardous liquid pipelines: fines up to $250,000 per violation, mandatory verification of operating pressures with testing or replacement, required shutoff valves, five-year internal inspections, and new fees. Their compliance costs are the public's safety gain, which is why the bill's defeat left them unchanged.

The bill repeals the exemption that let gas and hazardous liquid gathering lines in rural areas move product outside federal safety standards, bringing those lines under regulation one year after enactment.

industries.industry: Pipeline inspection and safety equipment makers
industries.note: Mandating a robotic internal inspection at least every five years, leak-detection standards, and automatic shutoff valves creates demand for the devices and services that meet those requirements.

Adding non-petroleum fuels and biofuels to the definition of hazardous liquid subjects those shipments to federal pipeline standards for the first time — new compliance costs, but safety rules for shipping flammable fuels.
